title: AS Paper 1 mock — Set B: Supply, prices and the dairy market
description: A full 80-mark AS Paper 1 (Theme 1: Introduction to markets and market failure) to be sat in 90 minutes. Section A has four multiple-choice and four short-answer questions on economic methodology, opportunity cost, economic systems, money, demand, cross elasticity and externalities (aim for about 20-25 minutes). Section B is a data response on a fictional country's dairy market covering elasticity of supply, supply shifts, price determination, producer surplus, minimum prices and the case for and against government intervention (about 65 minutes). Use the tables for calculations, draw full diagrams, and evaluate with a clear judgement in every 8+ mark answer. Designed to complement Set A so the two papers together cover all of Theme 1.

questions.prompt: A report on a proposal to raise university tuition fees contains four statements. Which one is a normative statement?
options: A A 10% rise in fees would reduce applications by around 2%.
B Graduates earn more over their working lives, on average, than non-graduates.
C It would be unfair to expect students from low-income families to pay higher fees.
D Universities' total fee revenue would rise if demand for places is price inelastic.
questions.explanation: A normative statement contains a value judgement and cannot be tested against evidence. 'Unfair' expresses an opinion about what ought to be. A, B and D are positive statements: each makes a claim that could, in principle, be checked against data, whether or not it turns out to be true.

questions.prompt: A farmer can use a field in one of three ways: grow wheat, earning a profit of £8,000; grow barley, earning a profit of £6,500; or rent it to a neighbour for £7,000. She chooses to grow wheat. What is the opportunity cost of growing wheat?
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, not the sum of all alternatives. The best option she gives up is renting the field for £7,000. A is the third-best option; C adds both rejected options together; D adds all three.

questions.prompt: The law of diminishing marginal utility helps to explain why:
options: A the demand curve for a good usually slopes downwards from left to right.
B the supply curve for a good usually slopes upwards from left to right.
C the demand curve for a normal good shifts to the right when incomes rise.
D a good with many close substitutes has price elastic demand.
questions.explanation: As a consumer buys more of a good, each extra unit adds less satisfaction, so they are only willing to buy more if the price falls. This gives an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: a downward-sloping demand curve. B relates to producers' costs, C is a shift caused by a non-price factor, and D is a determinant of PED.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of complete market failure (a missing market)?
options: A No private firm will supply a national defence system because it cannot charge those who benefit.
B The only petrol station in a remote village charges higher prices than stations in nearby towns.
C Smokers impose health costs on people who breathe in second-hand smoke.
D The price of strawberries falls every summer when the harvest is large.
questions.explanation: Complete market failure occurs when the market does not supply a good at all, creating a missing market, as with public goods such as national defence where non-excludability creates a free-rider problem. B and C are examples of partial market failure (the market exists but allocates resources inefficiently). D is the price mechanism working normally.

questions.prompt: Explain two disadvantages of a command economy, with reference to the views of Friedrich Hayek.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A command (planned) economy is one in which the state owns most resources and central planners decide what is produced, how it is produced and for whom, rather than prices set in markets.
Application/Analysis (any two): Information problem (Hayek): knowledge about consumers' wants and production conditions is dispersed among millions of people; in a market economy prices bring this information together, but planners cannot collect and process it, so they produce the wrong goods in the wrong quantities, causing persistent shortages and surpluses. Weak incentives: without the profit motive and competition, managers and workers have little reason to cut costs, improve quality or innovate, so productive and dynamic efficiency are low. Loss of freedom: Hayek argued in The Road to Serfdom that concentrating economic power in the state threatens individual liberty and consumer choice. Bureaucracy: planning requires large administrative costs and responds slowly to changes in demand.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of a command economy; 1 mark for identifying each of two relevant disadvantages (max 2); 1 mark for developing either disadvantage with explicit reference to Hayek's argument (for example that prices convey dispersed information that planners cannot replicate).

questions.prompt: In some towns, community schemes let members exchange services without using money; for example, an hour of plumbing is swapped for an hour of maths tutoring. Explain two functions of money that make exchange more efficient than this kind of barter.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The functions of money are a medium of exchange, a measure (unit) of value, a store of value and a method (standard) of deferred payment.
Application/Analysis (any two, linked to the weaknesses of barter): Medium of exchange: money is accepted in payment for any good or service, so it removes the need for a double coincidence of wants; the plumber no longer needs to find someone who both needs plumbing and offers something the plumber wants. Measure of value: prices in pounds allow the value of different services to be compared easily, whereas barter requires an exchange ratio for every pair of services (is an hour of plumbing worth one or two hours of tutoring?). Store of value: money can be saved and spent later, while an hour of labour cannot be stored. Method of deferred payment: debts can be agreed now and repaid later in money, enabling credit.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for identifying each of two functions of money (max 2); 1 mark for explaining how each function overcomes a specific weakness of barter (max 2).

questions.prompt: When the price of a coffee-pod machine falls from £120 to £96, monthly sales of compatible coffee pods rise from 50,000 boxes to 60,000 boxes. Calculate the cross elasticity of demand for coffee pods with respect to the price of the machine, and explain what your answer shows.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: XED = % change in quantity demanded of good A / % change in price of good B.
Application: % change in quantity of pods = (60,000 - 50,000) / 50,000 x 100 = +20%. % change in price of machines = (96 - 120) / 120 x 100 = -20%. XED = 20 / -20 = -1.0.
Analysis: The negative sign shows the goods are complements (jointly demanded): cheaper machines lead to more machines being bought and so more pods. A value of -1 shows a fairly strong relationship, with demand for pods changing proportionately to the change in machine price. This explains why firms may sell machines cheaply to increase profitable pod sales.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for the XED formula; 1 mark for both percentage changes; 1 mark for XED = -1.0; 1 mark for explaining that the negative sign shows the goods are complements (with comment on strength).

questions.prompt: Explain, using a diagram, why the free market may lead to under-consumption of vaccinations against seasonal flu.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A positive consumption externality is a benefit to third parties from consumption that is not reflected in the price; marginal social benefit (MSB) = marginal private benefit (MPB) + marginal external benefit, so MSB lies above MPB.
Application: A vaccinated person is less likely to infect family, colleagues and vulnerable people; fewer hospital admissions reduce pressure on the NHS; less staff absence benefits employers.
Analysis: Individuals consider only their private benefit, so the market reaches Qm where MPB = MPC, below the social optimum Q* where MSB = MSC. Too few vaccinations are consumed and there is a welfare loss (the triangle between MSB and MSC from Qm to Q*). Diagram: MPC = MSC upward sloping; MPB and MSB downward sloping with MSB above MPB; Qm and Q* marked; welfare loss shaded.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge of a positive externality (or MSB above MPB); 1 mark for an accurately labelled diagram showing Qm below Q*; 1 mark for application to flu vaccination (an identified external benefit); 1 mark for analysis explaining why individuals' decisions lead to under-consumption and a welfare loss.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the price elasticity of supply of milk between 2021 and 2022. With reference to Extract A, explain one reason why the supply of milk is so price inelastic.
questions.context:
Brenland's dairy market (illustrative data)

Table 1: The Brenland milk market, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Average farm-gate milk price (pence per litre) | Milk production (million litres) | Number of dairy farms | Animal feed price index (2021 = 100)
2021 | 30 | 14,000 | 8,200 | 100
2022 | 45 | 14,280 | 8,050 | 148
2023 | 41 | 14,420 | 7,900 | 132
2024 | 33 | 14,100 | 7,600 | 110
2025 | 36 | 13,800 | 7,350 | 104

Table 2: Brenland retail market for milk and milk alternatives (illustrative data)
Indicator | 2021 | 2025
Share of retail sales volume: cow's milk (%) | 93 | 88
Share of retail sales volume: plant-based drinks (%) | 7 | 12
Average supermarket price of cow's milk (pence per litre) | 80 | 95
Farm-gate price as a share of the supermarket price (%) | 37.5 | 37.9

Extract A: A rollercoaster for farmers
Brenland, a fictional country, is broadly self-sufficient in milk, but the farm-gate price (the price processors pay farmers) closely follows world dairy prices. In 2022 strong global demand for butter and milk powder coincided with a surge in the cost of animal feed, fertiliser and energy, and the farm-gate price rose to a record 45p per litre. Farmers could do little to raise output quickly: a calf takes around two years to become a milking cow, milking parlours are expensive to expand, and raw milk must be collected within a couple of days. By 2024, higher output in the major exporting countries and weaker demand from importers had pushed the price down to 33p, below the average cost of production of around 36p per litre on many family farms. At home, younger consumers have been switching to oat and soya drinks for health, environmental and animal-welfare reasons. A very dry summer in 2025 reduced grass growth, forcing farmers to buy in extra feed. Around 850 dairy farms have closed since 2021, mostly small family farms; many of their herds were bought by larger farms using automated milking systems.

Extract B: Should the government guarantee a price?
The Brenland Farmers' Union is campaigning for a guaranteed minimum farm-gate price of 38p per litre. Under its plan, a government agency would buy at 38p any milk that processors did not want, and turn it into butter and milk powder to be stored and sold later. The Union estimates that at 38p, production would be around 3% higher than in 2024 within two years, while purchases by processors would be around 1% lower. Treasury officials point out that when the European Economic Community guaranteed high prices for dairy products in the 1970s and 1980s, it built up large stores of surplus butter and milk powder, and eventually introduced milk production quotas in 1984. Supermarkets, which often sell milk cheaply to attract shoppers, warn that the plan would raise shelf prices. Alternative proposals include payments to farmers for environmental improvements such as planting hedgerows, help for farmers to agree fixed-price contracts with processors in advance, and an investigation by the competition authority into whether supermarkets and processors use their buying power to hold down farm-gate prices. Some economists argue that the government should not intervene at all, since the exit of high-cost farms allows resources to move to more efficient producers.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: PES = % change in quantity supplied / % change in price. Supply is price inelastic when PES is less than 1.
Application: % change in quantity supplied = (14,280 - 14,000) / 14,000 x 100 = +2%. % change in price = (45 - 30) / 30 x 100 = +50%. PES = 2 / 50 = 0.04 (highly price inelastic).
Analysis (any one reason from Extract A, developed): Time lag in production: a calf takes around two years to become a milking cow, so herds cannot be expanded quickly in response to a higher price. Capacity constraints: milking parlours are expensive to expand, so farms are close to full capacity in the short run. Perishability: raw milk must be collected within days and cannot be stockpiled, so farmers cannot release stored milk when prices rise. Credit may be given for noting that the figure assumes other supply factors were unchanged, whereas feed costs rose 48% in 2022, shifting supply left, so the true PES along the curve may be somewhat higher.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for the PES formula; 1 mark for both percentage changes; 1 mark for PES = 0.04; up to 2 marks for explaining one reason for inelastic supply using Extract A (1 for identification, 1 for development).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A change in a non-price factor causes a shift in the supply curve (an increase shifts it right, a decrease shifts it left), whereas a change in price causes a movement along it.
Application/Analysis (any two, using the data): Costs of production: the feed price index rose 48% in 2022 (100 to 148) and fertiliser and energy costs surged, raising the cost of producing each litre and shifting supply left; the index then fell to 104 by 2025, which would shift supply back to the right. Number of producers: around 850 farms (8,200 to 7,350) closed, reducing supply, although larger farms bought many herds. Weather: the dry summer of 2025 reduced grass growth, cutting yields and raising feed costs, shifting supply left (production fell to 13,800 million litres). Technology: automated milking systems on larger farms raise productivity and shift supply right.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for knowledge that non-price factors shift the supply curve; for each of two factors, 1 mark for identification and 1 mark for explanation of the direction of the shift supported by data from Table 1 or Extract A (max 4).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Equilibrium price is determined where demand equals supply; shifts in demand and supply create excess supply or demand that moves the price to a new equilibrium; non-price determinants of demand (tastes, substitutes, world demand) and supply (costs, output elsewhere).
Application: Farm-gate price fell from 45p to 33p (a fall of about 27%); feed price index fell from 148 to 110; higher output in major exporting countries; weaker world import demand; plant-based share of retail sales rose from 7% to 12% by 2025; Brenland prices follow world prices.
Analysis: Reason 1, supply increase: falling feed costs and expanded output by exporters shift supply to the right; at the old price there is excess supply, so processors bid down the price until a new, lower equilibrium is reached. Reason 2, demand decrease: weaker demand from importers and domestic substitution towards plant-based drinks (a change in tastes towards substitutes) shift demand to the left, creating excess supply at 45p and pushing the price down. Diagram: supply shifting right and/or demand shifting left, with equilibrium price falling from P1 to P2 and the quantity outcome explained (production in Brenland was broadly unchanged, consistent with both shifts operating together).
Evaluation: Relative importance: Brenland's price follows world prices, so global supply and demand probably matter more than domestic tastes; the plant-based shift is gradual (5 percentage points over four years) so it explains only a small part of a 27% fall. Part of the fall reverses the unusual 2022 spike rather than reflecting a permanent change. With inelastic supply (PES 0.04), even small shifts in demand cause large price changes. Judgement on which reason dominated.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 5 marks; Evaluation up to 3 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (5 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Analyses two distinct reasons, each with an accurate diagram and a clear chain from the shift to excess supply to a lower equilibrium price, uses the data (45p to 33p, feed index 148 to 110, 7% to 12%), and evaluates by judging which cause was more significant, linking to the very low PES and the role of world prices.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Producer surplus: the difference between the price producers receive and the minimum price at which they are willing to supply, shown as the area above the supply curve and below the price. The price mechanism's signalling, incentive and rationing functions reallocate resources between uses.
Application: Price fell from 45p to 33p per litre while production was 14,100 million litres in 2024, so producers lost roughly 12p x 14,100 million = around £1.7 billion of revenue on that output; average cost of around 36p on many family farms is above the 33p price; farm numbers fell from 8,050 to 7,600; larger farms with automated systems bought herds.
Analysis: Diagram: fall in price from P1 to P2 along (or with a shift of) the supply curve; producer surplus shrinks from the area above supply and below P1 to the smaller area below P2; the lost area is a rectangle (transferred to buyers) plus a small triangle. Resource allocation: the lower price signals that milk is less valued relative to other uses; reduced profit removes the incentive for high-cost farms to stay in production, so land, labour and capital move to other uses (for example beef, arable farming or non-farm uses) and output shifts to lower-cost, larger producers; lower prices help ration milk to processors and consumers who now face cheaper inputs.
Evaluation: Supply also shifted right as feed costs fell (index 148 to 110), so part of producers' lost surplus is offset by lower costs; the net fall is smaller than £1.7 billion. Effects differ between farms: large automated farms may still earn surplus while small family farms below 36p average cost make losses. Reallocation may take time because farm assets are specific and farmers may be reluctant to leave; consumers gain only if processors and supermarkets pass on lower prices, while the farm-gate share of the supermarket price stayed around 38%. Resource reallocation may improve efficiency but have social costs in rural areas. Judgement.

Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate producer surplus diagram with the lost area clearly identified, quantifies the loss using Table 1, explains through the signalling and incentive functions how resources move to more efficient producers, and evaluates by allowing for the simultaneous fall in feed costs, the different impact on large and small farms, and time lags in reallocation.

Treasury officials point out that when the European Economic Community guaranteed high prices for dairy products in the 1970s and 1980s, it built up large stores of surplus butter and milk powder, and eventually introduced milk production quotas in 1984. Supermarkets, which often sell milk cheaply to attract shoppers, warn that the plan would raise shelf prices. Alternative proposals include payments to farmers for environmental improvements such as planting hedgerows, help for farmers to agree fixed-price contracts with processors in advance, and an investigation by the competition authority into whether supermarkets and processors use their buying power to hold down farm-gate prices. Some economists argue that the government should not intervene at all, since the exit of high-cost farms allows resources to move to more efficient producers.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A minimum price is a legal floor set above the equilibrium price; it creates excess supply; with a guarantee, the government must buy the surplus (a buffer stock style scheme) and store or dispose of it.
Application: 38p is 5p above the 2024 price of 33p and above the 36p average cost of many family farms. Using 2024 output of 14,100 million litres: production would rise by around 3% to about 14,523 million litres while processors' purchases fall by about 1% to around 13,959 million litres, a surplus of around 564 million litres costing roughly £214 million a year at 38p (before any revenue from selling stored butter and powder). EEC surpluses and quotas in 1984; supermarkets' warning about shelf prices.
Analysis: Diagram: minimum price above equilibrium; quantity supplied rises and quantity demanded contracts, creating excess supply that the agency buys, with the cost to the government shown as the price times the surplus. Effects on farmers: higher and more stable incomes, fewer closures, more certainty for investment. Effects on consumers and processors: higher input costs passed on in higher shelf prices; consumers lose consumer surplus; may accelerate switching to plant-based drinks. Effects on the taxpayer: purchase and storage costs; opportunity cost of the spending. Allocative effects: the guarantee blocks the price signal that should move resources out of high-cost farms, encouraging over-production.
Evaluation: The size of the surplus depends on elasticities: supply is very inelastic in the short run (PES around 0.04 in 2021-22), so the surplus may be small at first but grow as farmers expand herds over two or more years, as happened in the EEC. If world prices recover above 38p the floor would cost nothing. Stored produce might be sold when prices rise, reducing net cost, but may also depress future prices. Effects on supermarket prices may be limited because the farm-gate price is under 40% of the shelf price. Judgement on whether the benefits for farmers outweigh the costs to consumers and taxpayers.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or one-sided, and diagrams may contain minor errors or not be explained.
KAA Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context, using the data selectively; analysis develops clear, logical, multi-step chains of reasoning, supported by accurate diagrams integrated into the answer where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluative comments are generic, asserted or unsupported by evidence; no clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Relevant evaluation that is supported by evidence from the extracts or wider knowledge, weighing arguments and reaching a reasoned judgement.
A* answer: Draws an accurate minimum price diagram with excess supply and government cost shown, calculates the likely surplus (around 564 million litres) and cost (around £214 million), assesses effects on farmers, consumers, taxpayers and resource allocation, and evaluates using elasticity over time, the EEC experience and the possibility that world prices make the floor non-binding, reaching a supported judgement.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether the government of Brenland should intervene in the dairy market to support farmers, or leave the farm-gate price to be determined by the free market.

Extract A: A rollercoaster for farmers
Brenland, a fictional country, is broadly self-sufficient in milk, but the farm-gate price (the price processors pay farmers) closely follows world dairy prices. In 2022 strong global demand for butter and milk powder coincided with a surge in the cost of animal feed, fertiliser and energy, and the farm-gate price rose to a record 45p per litre. Farmers could do little to raise output quickly: a calf takes around two years to become a milking cow, milking parlours are expensive to expand, and raw milk must be collected within a couple of days. By 2024, higher output in the major exporting countries and weaker demand from importers had pushed the price down to 33p, below the average cost of production of around 36p per litre on many family farms. At home, younger consumers have been switching to oat and soya drinks for health, environmental and animal-welfare reasons. A very dry summer in 2025 reduced grass growth, forcing farmers to buy in extra feed. Around 850 dairy farms have closed since 2021, mostly small family farms; many of their herds were bought by larger farms using automated milking systems.

Extract B: Should the government guarantee a price?
The Brenland Farmers' Union is campaigning for a guaranteed minimum farm-gate price of 38p per litre. Under its plan, a government agency would buy at 38p any milk that processors did not want, and turn it into butter and milk powder to be stored and sold later. The Union estimates that at 38p, production would be around 3% higher than in 2024 within two years, while purchases by processors would be around 1% lower. Treasury officials point out that when the European Economic Community guaranteed high prices for dairy products in the 1970s and 1980s, it built up large stores of surplus butter and milk powder, and eventually introduced milk production quotas in 1984. Supermarkets, which often sell milk cheaply to attract shoppers, warn that the plan would raise shelf prices. Alternative proposals include payments to farmers for environmental improvements such as planting hedgerows, help for farmers to agree fixed-price contracts with processors in advance, and an investigation by the competition authority into whether supermarkets and processors use their buying power to hold down farm-gate prices. Some economists argue that the government should not intervene at all, since the exit of high-cost farms allows resources to move to more efficient producers.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Free market allocation through the price mechanism (Adam Smith's invisible hand; Hayek's view that prices carry information); market failures in agriculture: price volatility from inelastic supply and demand, positive environmental externalities, information gaps, unequal bargaining power; methods of intervention (minimum prices, subsidies, regulation, competition policy); government failure.
Application: Price swings from 30p to 45p to 33p; PES of 0.04; 850 farm closures; family farms' average cost around 36p; larger automated farms buying herds; plant-based share rising; Farmers' Union's 38p floor and estimated surplus; EEC surpluses and quotas; alternatives in Extract B: environmental payments, fixed-price contracts, competition investigation; supermarkets selling milk cheaply; farm-gate share of the shelf price around 38%.
Analysis: Case for leaving it to the market: falling prices signal that resources should move from high-cost to lower-cost farms, raising productive efficiency; larger farms with automation lower costs; intervention distorts price signals and creates surpluses and taxpayer costs. Case for intervention: inelastic supply makes prices volatile, so farmers face risk that discourages investment; farm exits are hard to reverse because herds and skills are lost; farming provides positive externalities (landscape, hedgerows, rural communities) not rewarded by the price; supermarkets and processors may hold down prices using buying power. Targeted interventions: environmental payments correct a positive externality without encouraging over-production; fixed-price contracts reduce volatility through the market; a competition investigation addresses imbalance of power.
Evaluation: Whether intervention is justified depends on the cause of low prices: if world supply and changing tastes (a permanent shift) drive them, support delays inevitable adjustment; if volatility and buying power are the problem, targeted measures are appropriate. Government failure risks: the 38p floor repeats EEC-style surpluses and costs around £214 million a year; information gaps make the 'right' floor hard to set; political pressure makes schemes hard to remove. Time: adjustment through exit is slow and has social costs in rural areas. Distribution: price support mostly benefits the largest farms producing the most milk. Prioritised judgement, for example: reject a price floor but use environmental payments, contract support and a competition investigation.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis (KAA) up to 12 marks; Evaluation up to 8 marks.
Levels:
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated knowledge, often limited to definitions; little or no application to the context; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Mostly accurate knowledge with some application to the context and data; chains of reasoning are partial or not clearly linked to the question; diagrams, if used, contain errors or are not explained.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with relevant use of data from the extracts; several developed chains of reasoning, though some lack depth or balance; diagrams are mostly accurate and referred to.
KAA Level 4 (10-12 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout, integrating data from the extracts; fully developed, coherent chains of reasoning covering both sides of the issue; accurate diagrams are integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluative comments are generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; no supported judgement.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation addresses relevant issues with some support from the extracts, but is not fully developed, not prioritised or lacks a clear final judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-8 marks): Sustained, well-supported evaluation that weighs the arguments, prioritises the most significant factors, recognises what the answer depends on and reaches a fully justified judgement.
A* answer: Weighs the efficiency case for the free market against specific market failures in the dairy sector, using data throughout (PES 0.04, price swings, farm closures, surplus cost), compares a minimum price with the targeted alternatives in Extract B, explicitly considers government failure and the EEC evidence, and reaches a clear, conditional judgement on which form of intervention, if any, is best.
